 "diagnosis": "The loop invariants only describe the prefix b[0..next) (b's in [0,white), a's in [white,next)) and say nothing about the suffix b[blue..|b|), where the loop moves every 'd'. At exit next == blue, but the invariants give no information about b[blue..], so Dafny cannot conclude sortedbad(b) for the whole string (e.g. it cannot rule out a 'b' after position blue). The counterexample (next=0, blue=|b|... ) reflects that the suffix is unconstrained. Fix: add the invariant forall i :: blue <= i < |b| ==> b[i] == 'd'."}
EOF
python3 - <<'EOF'
p='program.dfy'
s=open(p).read()
s=s.replace("""    invariant forall i :: white <= i < next ==> b[i] == 'a';
""","""    invariant forall i :: white <= i < next ==> b[i] == 'a';
    invariant forall i :: blue <= i < |b| ==> b[i] == 'd';
""")
open(p,'w').write(s)
EOF
dafny verify program.dfy

Dafny now verifies `program.dfy`: "4 verified, 0 errors". The command still exits with code 2. That's not a verification failure: the file has a lot of old-style warnings (unneeded semicolons, and indentation in `sortedbad` that Dafny suspects is missing parentheses), and this Dafny setup counts warnings as a build failure. I left those warnings alone. Pass `--allow-warnings` if you want a clean exit code.

**Diagnosis** (saved in `diagnosis.json`): the failing piece was a loop invariant, at the bridge step (the invariants plus the exit condition didn't imply the postcondition). The loop's invariants only described the front of the string, `b[0..next)`: `'b'`s in `[0, white)` and `'a'`s in `[white, next)`. Nothing described the back part, `b[blue..|b|)`, where the loop moves every `'d'`. When the loop ends, `next == blue`, but Dafny knew nothing about that back part. So it couldn't rule out, say, a `'b'` sitting after an `'a'`, and couldn't prove `sortedbad(b)`.

**Fix:** I added one invariant at `program.dfy:31`:
```dafny
invariant forall i :: blue <= i < |b| ==> b[i] == 'd';
```
It holds when the loop starts (the back part is empty because `blue == |b|`). It stays true each time a `'d'` is swapped to position `blue - 1`. With it, at exit the whole string is `'b'`s, then `'a'`s, then `'d'`s, which proves the postcondition.
